strengths: MSAM offers a simple, practically useful way to reuse momentum for parameter perturbations with one forward/backward pass per update. Its reported speed is 0.99 relative to the base optimizer, versus 0.52 for SAM.

The empirical gains over base optimizers are meaningful and reasonably broad. On CIFAR100, MSAM improves WRN-16-4 accuracy from 76.90% to 79.11%; ImageNet experiments cover both ResNets and vision transformers. Adaptive and BatchNorm-only extensions further demonstrate compatibility with existing techniques.

The ablations investigate perturbation sign, normalization, learning-rate scaling, alternative directions, and equal computational budgets. The observation that decoupling perturbation magnitude from the learning-rate schedule matters more than normalization provides useful insight into the relationship with Nesterov acceleration.

The algorithm and experimental presentation are generally clear. Hyperparameter scans, a public code link, and candid discussion of instability and computational constraints support reproducibility. No material research ethics concerns are evident.
weaknesses: The theoretical justification in Appendix A.1 is incorrect as stated. Proposition 1 fails when the mean Hessian curvature is negative: for H = -I, its left-hand side is greater than -rho², contradicting the claimed upper bound. Setting 1 does not exclude negative mean curvature. Theorem 3 also does not establish the assumptions needed to transfer a Gaussian-perturbed population-risk bound to the unperturbed predictor or control the Taylor remainder. Consequently, the claimed generalization guarantee remains unsupported.

The main SAM comparison uses unequal warm-up treatment despite evidence that the same modification benefits SAM. Table A.1 shows that disabling SAM during warm-up improves accuracy from 69.2% to 69.8%, versus MSAM's 69.1%, yet this stronger SAM setting is omitted from the main comparisons. Table 2 also contains substantial gaps: 75.8% versus 78.2% for ViT-S/16 at 300 epochs and 75.7% versus 77.7% for ViT-B/16. Equal-compute ImageNet evidence covers only ViT-S/32, limiting the broader claim of comparable performance.

Hyperparameter selection and statistical support need clarification. Appendix A.6 reports the best perturbation strength from curves labeled test accuracy without documenting a separate validation split, leaving potential test-set selection bias unresolved. Most ImageNet results use single runs, with uncertainty inferred from smaller baseline models rather than the corresponding method/model combinations. Those estimates cannot substantiate close rankings or equivalence claims.

The sharpness interpretation exceeds what the diagnostic experiments establish. Figure 3 projects MSAM gradients into the SAM/SGD plane, discarding components that could substantially change their actual agreement. Directional sharpness and curvature measurements, concentrated on WRN-16-4/CIFAR100, do not establish approximation of the full-neighborhood sharpness objective. Given the close relationship to Nesterov extrapolation, the paper needs a more precise separation between its useful scheduling insight and its stronger sharpness-minimization claims.

Some reproduction details remain incomplete: timing results omit GPU specifications and model-specific measurements; default momentum and AdamW settings are not fully stated; and Algorithm 1 normalizes an initially zero momentum vector without specifying handling. The practical results are promising, but the unresolved theoretical and comparative-evaluation issues outweigh them in the current submission.
